Main article: [Bids for the 2004 Summer Olympics](/wiki/Bids_for_the_2004_Summer_Olympics "Bids for the 2004 Summer Olympics")

[Athens](/wiki/Athens "Athens") was chosen as the host city during the 106th IOC Session held in [Lausanne](/wiki/Lausanne "Lausanne"), Switzerland, on 5 September 1997. The Greek capital had lost its bid to organize the [1996 Summer Olympics](/wiki/1996_Summer_Olympics "1996 Summer Olympics") to the American city of [Atlanta](/wiki/Atlanta "Atlanta") nearly seven years before, during the 96th IOC Session in Tokyo, Japan on 18 September 1990. Under the direction of [Gianna Angelopoulos-Daskalaki](/wiki/Gianna_Angelopoulos-Daskalaki "Gianna Angelopoulos-Daskalaki"), Athens pursued another bid, this time for the right to host the Summer Olympics in 2004. The success of Athens in securing the 2004 Games was based largely on the bid's appeal to human values, the history of the Games from ancient age and modern age and the emphasis that Athens is placed at the pivotal role that Greece and Athens could play in promoting the Modern Olympism and the Olympic Movement.[[7]](#cite_note-9) Unlike the 1996 bid that was seen arrogant when the city was bidding, the 2004 bid was lauded for its low scale, humility, honest and earnestness, its focused message, and a more real and detailed bid concept.[[8]](#cite_note-10)

During the unsuccessful 1996 bid, concerns and criticisms were raised – primarily regarding critical subjects about the city's infrastructural readiness, its air pollution, its budget and politicization of the Games' events and their preparations.[[9]](#cite_note-11) The subsequent successful organization of other events such as the [1991 Mediterranean Games](/wiki/1991_Mediterranean_Games "1991 Mediterranean Games"), the [1994 FIVB Volleyball Men's World Championship](/wiki/1994_FIVB_Volleyball_Men%27s_World_Championship "1994 FIVB Volleyball Men's World Championship"), [1994 World

Elwood Doherty, a Curtiss pilot,[[162]](#cite_note-170) coaxes the structurally modified [Langley Aerodrome](/wiki/Langley_Aerodrome "Langley Aerodrome") into the air above the surface of [Keuka Lake](/wiki/Keuka_Lake "Keuka Lake") near [Hammondsport, New York](/wiki/Hammondsport,_New_York "Hammondsport, New York"), September 17, 1914.

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9f/430-L1-S1_640.jpg/330px-430-L1-S1_640.jpg)](/wiki/File:430-L1-S1_640.jpg)

Pieces of fabric and wood from the 1903 *[Wright Flyer](/wiki/Wright_Flyer "Wright Flyer")* traveled to the Moon in the [Apollo 11](/wiki/Apollo_11 "Apollo 11") [Lunar Module *Eagle*](/wiki/Lunar_Module_Eagle "Lunar Module Eagle"), and are exhibited at the [Wright Brothers National Memorial](/wiki/Wright_Brothers_National_Memorial "Wright Brothers National Memorial").

[S. P. Langley](/wiki/Samuel_Pierpont_Langley "Samuel Pierpont Langley"), secretary of [the Smithsonian Institution](/wiki/The_Smithsonian_Institution "The Smithsonian Institution") from 1887 until his death in 1906, experimented for years with model flying machines and successfully flew unmanned powered fixed-wing model aircraft in 1896 and 1903. Two tests of his manned full-size motor-driven Aerodrome in October and December 1903, however, were complete failures. Nevertheless, the Smithsonian later proudly displayed the Aerodrome in its museum as the first heavier-than-air craft "capable" of manned powered flight, relegating the Wright brothers' invention to secondary status and triggering a decades-long feud with Orville Wright, whose brother had received help from the Smithsonian when beginning his own quest for flight.[[h]](#cite_note-171)

Steve Chen :: Early life and education :: chunk_0001
Chen was born in [Taipei](/wiki/Taipei "Taipei"), [Taiwan](/wiki/Taiwan "Taiwan"). When he was seven years old, he and his family immigrated to the United States in 1986[[3]](#cite_note-3) and settled in [Arlington Heights, Illinois](/wiki/Arlington_Heights,_Illinois "Arlington Heights, Illinois").[[4]](#cite_note-4) He went to [Thomas Middle School](/wiki/Arlington_Heights_School_District_25 "Arlington Heights School District 25") in [Arlington Heights](/wiki/Arlington_Heights,_Illinois "Arlington Heights, Illinois") for his middle school education and [John Hersey High School](/wiki/John_Hersey_High_School "John Hersey High School") in [Arlington Heights](/wiki/Arlington_Heights,_Illinois "Arlington Heights, Illinois") for his freshman year of high school. For his final three years of high school, he attended the [Illinois Mathematics and Science Academy](/wiki/Illinois_Mathematics_and_Science_Academy "Illinois Mathematics and Science Academy") in [Aurora, Illinois](/wiki/Aurora,_Illinois "Aurora, Illinois"). After graduating from high school, Chen was educated at the [University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign](/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Urbana-Champaign "University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign"), where he studied [computer science](/wiki/Computer_science "Computer science"),[[5]](#cite_note-5) then decided to leave the university in 1999 in order to go to [Silicon Valley](/wiki/Silicon_Valley "Silicon Valley").[[6]](#cite_note-6)

Map of the Bordeaux regions with most of its appellations shown. The rivers Garonne and Dordogne, and the Gironde estuary are important in defining the various parts of the region.

**Bordeaux wine** ([Occitan](/wiki/Occitan_language "Occitan language"): *vin de Bordèu*; [French](/wiki/French_language "French language"): *vin de Bordeaux*) is produced in the [Bordeaux region](/wiki/Bordeaux_wine_regions "Bordeaux wine regions") of southwest [France](/wiki/France "France"), around the city of [Bordeaux](/wiki/Bordeaux "Bordeaux"), on the [Garonne River](/wiki/Garonne "Garonne"). To the north of the city, the [Dordogne River](/wiki/Dordogne_(river) "Dordogne (river)") joins the [Garonne](/wiki/Garonne "Garonne") forming the broad estuary called the [Gironde](/wiki/Gironde_estuary "Gironde estuary"); the [Gironde](/wiki/Gironde "Gironde") department, with a total vineyard area of 110,800 hectares,[[1]](#cite_note-1) is the second largest wine-growing area in France behind the Languedoc-Rousillon.[[2]](#cite_note-2)

Average vintages produce over 700 million bottles of wine, ranging from large quantities of daily [table wine](/wiki/Table_wine "Table wine") to some of the world's most expensive and prestigious wines. The vast majority of wine produced in Bordeaux is red (sometimes called "claret" in Britain), with sweet white wines (most notably [Sauternes](/wiki/Sauternes_(wine) "Sauternes (wine)")), dry whites, and (in much smaller quantities) rosé and sparkling wines ([Crémant de Bordeaux](/wiki/Cr%C3%A9mant_de_Bordeaux "Crémant de Bordeaux")) collectively making up the remainder. Bordeaux wine is made by more than 5,660 producers or *[châteaux](/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teau "Château")*. There are 65 [appellations](/wiki/Appellation_d%27origine_contr%C3%B4l%C3

Main article: [Geography of Pennsylvania](/wiki/Geography_of_Pennsylvania "Geography of Pennsylvania")

Further information: [List of counties in Pennsylvania](/wiki/List_of_counties_in_Pennsylvania "List of counties in Pennsylvania")

Pennsylvania is 170 miles (274 km) north to south and 283 miles (455 km) east to west.[[83]](#cite_note-87) Of a total 46,055 square miles (119,282 km2),[[5]](#cite_note-geo_census_2010-5) 44,817 square miles (116,075 km2) are land, 490 square miles (1,269 km2) are inland waters, and 749 square miles (1,940 km2) are waters in [Lake Erie](/wiki/Lake_Erie "Lake Erie").[[84]](#cite_note-88) It is the [33rd-largest state](/wiki/List_of_U.S._states_by_area "List of U.S. states by area") in the United States.[[85]](#cite_note-89) Pennsylvania has 51 miles (82 km)[[86]](#cite_note-90) of coastline along Lake Erie and 57 miles (92 km)[[12]](#cite_note-NOAA_Office_of_Coastal_Management-15) of shoreline along the [Delaware Estuary](/wiki/Delaware_River "Delaware River"). Of the original [Thirteen Colonies](/wiki/Thirteen_Colonies "Thirteen Colonies"), Pennsylvania is the only state that does not border the [Atlantic Ocean](/wiki/Atlantic_Ocean "Atlantic Ocean"). With 86,000 miles of rivers and streams, Pennsylvania has the highest density of waterways of any state in the continental United States.[[87]](#cite_note-91)[[88]](#cite_note-92)

The boundaries of the state are the [Mason–Dixon line](/wiki/Mason%E2%80%93Dixon_line "Mason–Dixon line") (39°43' N) to the south, [Twelve-Mile Circle](/wiki/Twelve-Mile_Circle "Twelve-Mile Circle") on the Pennsylvania-[Delaware](/wiki/Delaware "Delaware") border, the [Delaware River](/wiki/Delaware_River "Delaware River") to the east, 80°31' W to the west, and the [42° N](/wiki/42nd_parallel_north "42nd parallel north") to the north, except for a short segment on the western end where a [triangle](/wiki/Erie_Triangle "Erie Triangle") extends north to Lake Erie. [Ruth Bader Ginsburg](/wiki/Ruth_Bader_Ginsburg "Ruth Bader Ginsburg") giving testimony before the Senate Judiciary Committee during the 1993 hearings on her nomination to be an associate justice

Not every Supreme Court [nominee](/wiki/Nominee#Noun "Nominee") has received a floor vote in the Senate. A president may withdraw a nomination before an actual confirmation vote occurs, typically because it is clear that the Senate will reject the nominee; this occurred with President George W. Bush's nomination of [Harriet Miers](/wiki/Harriet_Miers "Harriet Miers") in 2005. The Senate may also fail to act on a nomination, which expires at the end of the session. President [Dwight Eisenhower](/wiki/Dwight_Eisenhower "Dwight Eisenhower")'s first nomination of [John Marshall Harlan II](/wiki/John_Marshall_Harlan_II "John Marshall Harlan II") in November 1954 was not acted on by the Senate; Eisenhower re-nominated Harlan in January 1955, and Harlan was confirmed two months later. Most recently, the Senate failed to act on the March 2016 nomination of Merrick Garland, as the nomination expired in January 2017, and the vacancy was filled by Neil Gorsuch, an [appointee](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/appointee "wikt:appointee") of President Trump.[[12]](#cite_note-SCnoms-12)
